newsitem.title: USA: Clinton will meet Republicans half way on budget.
newsitem.headline: Clinton will meet Republicans half way on budget.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Thursday his new budget proposal would balance the federal budget by the year 2002 and he would meet the Republicans "half way" on reaching that goal.

Sounding a conciliatory note, as he has often done since winning re-election, Clinton, a Democrat, pledged to work with the Republican-controlled Congress but gave few details on his fiscal 1998 budget proposal, due to be released on Feb. 6.

"I think this budget will show that I am making a clear effort to reach out to them and meet them half way to get this job done," Clinton told reporters at a White House event to announce a drop in student loan default rates.
"I also expect there to be a negotiating process with the Congress, and I will work with them in good faith as I have said all along," Clinton said.

"If the atmosphere of this Congress reflects what happened in the last two months of the last Congress, I think the American people will get their balanced budget," he added. "The atmosphere so far feels good to me."

Asked if he had made all his final budget decisions and if there was any chance of reopening them, specifically the Medicare health care programme for the elderly, Clinton said: "I have completed some time ago the work on the budget. We still ... have to work around the edges from time to time."

Medicare, which funds health care for 37 million people, is a politically charged subject because of Clinton's success during the 1996 election campaign in tarring the Republicans for their proposals to reduce the program's costs.

This week, officials said Clinton had told the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to draft his new budget without raising Medicare premiums, preferring to hold back such a potentially conciliatory gesture to the Republicans.

One official also said the OMB was also operating under the assumption that Medicare's burgeoning home health care costs will be shifted from the Hospital Insurance trust fund to a separate account with access to general tax revenues.

Republicans, as well as some independent analysts, have criticised this as a gimmick, arguing that while it would help maintain the solvency of the Medicare trust fund, it would not address the underlying issue of curbing the program's growth.
The Washington Post on Thursday reported that the Medicare decisions could be revisited.

Brookings Institute budget analyst Robert Reischauer said it would not be possible to integrate any change in Clinton's Medicare stance into the fiscal 1998 budget and still deliver it to Congress as scheduled by Feb. 6.
